title: A field of escape with no headquarters, no timetable, and no way to count its own passengers
register: documentary, distrustful of the tidy map
summary: It had no charter, no membership roll, and no national treasury: a changing field of self-emancipation, sustained by free Black churches, vigilance committees, sailors, and paid strangers who forwarded a person one leg at a time, often without knowing the next one. What moved was people, letters, money, and warnings, through commercial freight as often as secret houses, against a counter-network of marshals and slave catchers that was better funded and more formally chartered than any part of the Railroad itself. It did not dissolve; slavery ended piecemeal by state, by battle line, and finally by the Thirteenth Amendment on 6 December 1865, and its people moved into refugee relief, the Union army, and Reconstruction politics.

nodes.name: Dorchester and Caroline Counties, Maryland
nodes.note: Source region for Harriet Tubman's own escape and her roughly thirteen documented return expeditions between 1850 and 1860, built on family knowledge, kinship, and Black maritime labor along the peninsula.

nodes.name: Washington, D.C.
nodes.note: Thomas Smallwood and Charles Torrey organized multiple group removals from here in 1842-44; the publicity that made their operation famous also exposed it, and Torrey died in a Maryland penitentiary in 1846.

nodes.name: The Pearl, Potomac River
nodes.note: In 1848 seventy-seven enslaved people attempted a mass escape from Washington by schooner down the Potomac. Adverse winds delayed the vessel; a posse captured it, and many aboard were sold south.

nodes.name: Richmond
nodes.note: Henry Brown's 1849 self-shipment to Philadelphia began here, the clearest documented case of a freedom seeker exploiting ordinary commercial freight rather than a dedicated escape route.

nodes.name: Charleston
nodes.note: A harbor supporting stowaway and sailor-assisted escape against heavy customs and maritime enforcement. Robert Smalls seized the Confederate transport Planter here in 1862, a wartime maritime self-emancipation that belongs to the Railroad's military transformation.

nodes.name: Cincinnati
nodes.note: River crossings, a large free Black population, and abolitionist presses made Cincinnati a major node. Levi and Catharine Coffin ran a free-labor goods warehouse here from 1847 while aiding fugitives.

nodes.name: Ripley
nodes.note: John Rankin's house above the Ohio River is documented through family testimony and correspondence. John Parker, born enslaved and later a Black ironworker and foundry owner here, crossed into Kentucky to assist others; exact totals for either man remain estimates.

nodes.name: Newport, Fountain City
nodes.note: Levi and Catharine Coffin's earlier home, a well-attested forwarding point before their move to Cincinnati in 1847. Coffin's 1876 memoir presents him, in his own retrospective words, as the Railroad's "reputed president."

nodes.name: Philadelphia
nodes.note: A major receiving, documentation, and fundraising hub. William Still's Vigilance Committee assisted about one hundred people annually through the documented 1850s, mostly young men from Virginia and Maryland, a local recorded rate rather than a national one.

nodes.name: Wilmington, Delaware
nodes.note: Joined Eastern Shore and Maryland departures to Philadelphia. Thomas Garrett corresponded with Still and assisted many arrivals; in 1848 he and John Hunn were held civilly liable for helping the Hawkins family.

nodes.name: New York City
nodes.note: Simultaneously a refuge, a transit hub, and a kidnapping market. David Ruggles, secretary of the Committee of Vigilance, monitored the wharves, resisted kidnapping, and aided Frederick Douglass after his 1838 escape.

nodes.name: Albany
nodes.note: Stephen Myers, newspaper editor and vigilance operator, worked the Hudson-Erie corridor from here; recollections describing a fixed Washington-to-Oswego chain through Albany overstate the regularity of local traffic.

nodes.name: Syracuse
nodes.note: Jermain Wesley Loguen, a formerly enslaved minister, was an important correspondent and receiver; the 1851 rescue of Jerry Henry from federal custody happened here.

nodes.name: Rochester
nodes.note: Frederick Douglass published The North Star here from 1847 and hosted, funded, and corresponded on behalf of freedom seekers; his house burned in 1872, destroying many papers.

nodes.name: Boston
nodes.note: Successive vigilance committees supplied lodging, legal defense, and, at times, armed resistance; the 1850 Committee of Vigilance and Safety left account books documenting a functioning treasury, including a $100 payment in October 1853 to Austin Bearse for rescuing Sandy Swan from the harbor.

nodes.name: New Bedford
nodes.note: A whaling port with a substantial Black community giving relative anonymity and maritime employment; Frederick and Anna Douglass lived here after his escape.

nodes.name: Buffalo and Niagara Falls
nodes.modern: Buffalo and Niagara Falls, New York
nodes.note: Ferries, bridges, small craft, and winter ice offered several border crossings into Canada; Niagara was famous but far from the only terminal.

nodes.name: Detroit and Windsor
nodes.note: Before Upper Canada's early-nineteenth-century restriction on importing enslaved people, escape across the Detroit River could run southward into Michigan; after 1834's imperial emancipation the dominant flow reversed decisively northward.

nodes.name: St. Catharines
nodes.note: Harriet Tubman's residence for much of the 1850s, a staging point for family reunification and settlement rather than merely an endpoint.

nodes.name: Chatham
nodes.note: Supported churches, political conventions, and Mary Ann Shadd's Provincial Freeman; hosted John Brown's 1858 constitutional convention.

nodes.name: Dawn Settlement, Dresden
nodes.note: Josiah Henson and associates developed the British-American Institute here, a post-arrival community and institutional extension of the escape network rather than only an endpoint.

nodes.name: Elgin, Buxton Settlement
nodes.note: Founded in 1849 by Reverend William King and fifteen formerly enslaved people on a 9,000-acre tract organized through a joint-stock company; settlers bought fifty-acre farms and built schools, churches, and roads.

nodes.name: Texas-Mexico borderlands
nodes.note: Freedom seekers from Texas and the Southwest crossed the Rio Grande toward Mexican settlements after Mexico's 1829 national abolition, subject to a temporary Texas exemption. Routes ran south and southwest, contrary to the canonical northward map, and are less documented than the Ohio-Canada corridor.

nodes.name: William Still
nodes.note: Secretary and agent of the Philadelphia Vigilance Committee. Interviewed arrivals, preserved names and family details, raised and disbursed money, and corresponded with downstream agents; his journal of 25 December 1852 to 22 February 1857 is the most important surviving documentary record from an operational hub, published in full in 1872.

nodes.name: David Ruggles
nodes.note: Secretary of the New York Committee of Vigilance from its 1835 organization. Monitored the waterfront, resisted kidnapping, and aided Frederick Douglass after his 1838 escape.

nodes.name: Thomas Smallwood
nodes.note: Washington organizer and, under the pseudonym "Sam Weller," the earliest documented user of "under ground rail-road" in print, in the Albany Tocsin of Liberty on 10 August 1842.

nodes.name: Charles Turner Torrey
nodes.note: Organized repeated Washington-area group removals with Smallwood in 1842-44; captured and died in a Maryland penitentiary in 1846, exposing the danger of publicized repeated missions.

nodes.name: John Parker
nodes.note: Born enslaved, later a Black ironworker and foundry owner in Ripley who made repeated cross-river rescue expeditions into Kentucky.

nodes.name: Levi and Catharine Coffin
nodes.note: Aided fugitives first at Newport (now Fountain City), Indiana, then from 1847 at Cincinnati while running a free-labor goods warehouse. Coffin's 1876 memoir claims a retrospective total of 3,000 people aided; the figure is his own estimate, not a surviving passenger register.

nodes.name: Thomas Garrett
nodes.note: Quaker merchant who corresponded with William Still and assisted many arrivals; held civilly liable with John Hunn in 1848 for helping the Hawkins family.

nodes.name: Jermain Wesley Loguen
nodes.note: Syracuse minister, formerly enslaved himself, and resistance leader in the corridor running from the Hudson through the Erie Canal towns to the lakes.

nodes.name: Frederick Douglass
nodes.note: Escaped through commercial transport in 1838 and was aided in New York by David Ruggles; later published The North Star from Rochester and hosted, funded, and corresponded on behalf of others' escapes.

nodes.name: Lewis and Harriet Hayden
nodes.note: Boston shelter providers and militant opponents of rendition, whose Beacon Hill home is documented through vigilance committee accounts.

nodes.name: Austin Bearse
nodes.note: Boston mariner and harbor rescue operator; a documented Committee payment of $100 in October 1853 records his role in the rescue of Sandy Swan.

nodes.name: Harriet Tubman
nodes.note: Escaped from Maryland in 1849 and made roughly thirteen documented return expeditions between 1850 and 1860. The National Park Service records about seventy people she directly led out and fifty to sixty more she advised, well short of the older "three hundred" tradition; her wartime Combahee River role in 1863 was a separate, Union military operation.

nodes.name: Henry Box Brown
nodes.note: Shipped himself from Richmond to Philadelphia in a wooden crate via Adams Express Company on 23-24 March 1849, remaining confined roughly twenty-seven hours; his method worked once, but publicity made it unusable and exposed his accomplices.

nodes.name: William and Ellen Craft
nodes.note: Escaped from Georgia in 1848 by rail and steamboat, Ellen disguised as a white male enslaver; the 1850 Fugitive Slave Act exposed them to recapture in Boston and they ultimately moved to Britain.

nodes.name: Robert Smalls
nodes.note: Seized the Confederate transport Planter at Charleston with family members aboard in 1862 and delivered it to Union forces, a wartime maritime self-emancipation belonging to the Railroad's military-transformation phase.

nodes.name: Seth Concklin
nodes.note: Attempted to rescue Peter Still's family; captured and found dead while being transported back north in 1851, under circumstances still unresolved between murder and suicide.

nodes.name: The Fugitive Slave Act of 1850
nodes.note: Enacted 18 September 1850, it authorized federal commissioners, denied a jury trial in the summary rendition proceeding, and paid commissioners $10 for issuing a certificate against $5 for declining. It nationalized coercive recovery and, by intensifying risk, pushed migration further north into Canada.

nodes.name: The counter-network
nodes.note: Enslavers, professional slave catchers, federal marshals, commissioners, jailers, and reward-publishing newspapers formed a rival, better-chartered information and coercion network that also kidnapped free Black people where testimony was legally restricted.

nodes.name: The Union Army and contraband policy
nodes.note: Benjamin Butler's 1861 "contraband of war" designation at Fort Monroe supplied a military rationale for refusing Confederate claimants; confiscation acts, the Emancipation Proclamation, and Black enlistment progressively absorbed the civilian clandestine network into military and refugee systems.

nodes.name: Adams Express Company freight line
nodes.note: Ordinary commercial freight infrastructure that carried Henry Brown's box by wagon, railroad, steamboat, and ferry; a one-time appropriation of a route with no dedicated abolitionist chain behind it.

nodes.name: Coastal and river maritime traffic
nodes.note: Sailors and stewards could convey messages, provide concealment, or identify friendly boardinghouses; maritime arrivals in the thirty years before the Civil War are conservatively reconstructed at fifteen to twenty thousand, still an inferential figure.

nodes.name: Free Black churches and benevolent societies
nodes.note: African Methodist Episcopal, Baptist, and other Black congregations, mutual-aid societies, and boardinghouses supplied meeting places, donors, meals, nursing, and neighborhood intelligence largely without committee office or formal recognition. Earlier histories systematically undercounted this structural, not peripheral, layer.

edges.note: Attempted the rescue independently; found dead while being transported north, cause unresolved.
Prompted reorganization of the Boston Committee of Vigilance and Safety that same year.
Authorized federal commissioners and penalties for assistance, giving the recovery system formal statutory chartering the Railroad itself never had.

Kidnapping of free Black residents and pursuit of freedom seekers operated wherever slavery's border ran, not only in one place; positioned here as the network's point of origin under the 1793 federal act.
